summary: Age 8–9 pupils measure and estimate mass (g, kg) and liquid volume (l, ml) and solve one-step word problems in the same unit. The load-bearing hazard is scale-reading treated as COUNTING marks: children give each line the status of a unit instead of working out what each INTERVAL (space) is worth. Estimation only becomes meaningful once a child has a bodily referent for a gram, kilogram and litre. Guidance here couples (1) reading scales whose interval changes between tasks so pupils must re-decode the step, with (2) estimate-then-measure against physical benchmark objects. Static labelled pictures and recognition-only checks can scaffold or probe but do not require the child to decode a novel interval or calibrate an estimate against feedback.
misconceptions: Counts the marks/lines as units ('measuring is counting'), so reads a scale by the number of small marks rather than the interval value.
Assumes each small interval equals 1 (or 10) when the scale actually steps in 2s, 5s, 20s or 50s.
Reads the nearest labelled number to the level (endpoint reading) without noticing the level falls between marks, or ignores where the scale starts.
Estimates with no sense of the unit (a textbook '5 kg') or picks the wrong unit (grams for a person's mass).

activities.title: Decode the changing scale
steps: Before reading any value, find two labelled numbers on the jug (or balance) and count the gaps between them.
Work out what one small step is worth, e.g. 100 over 5 gaps = steps of 20.
Read a part-filled scale by accumulating the steps from where the scale starts, not by counting lines (e.g. a level at the labelled 300 plus two more 20-steps = 340 ml).
Use a small number line of the steps (0, 20, 40, 60…) to track the accumulated value when the interval is unlabelled, counting up from where the scale starts.
Repeat across tasks where the interval changes each time — 10 ml, 20 ml, 25 ml, 50 ml — so memorising a single step size fails.
Say aloud 'what is one small step worth?' every time before giving a reading.
activities.insight: The marks mean nothing until you decode the step: the same mark position (e.g. the 3rd small mark above a label) stands for different amounts on scales with different intervals, so measuring is working out interval value, not counting lines.

activities.title: Estimate first, then measure, against a real referent
steps: Hold a 1 kg bag of sugar, a 100 g weight, and a 1-litre bottle to build a felt sense of each unit.
For a target object (e.g. a textbook), commit to an estimate of its mass BEFORE measuring, saying whether it is heavier or lighter than the 1 kg bag.
Choose the sensible unit for the object — grams or kilograms, ml or litres — and justify it against a benchmark.
Measure the object and compare the true value with the estimate, noting the gap.
Repeat with several objects so the felt sense of each unit sharpens.
activities.insight: An estimate is a comparison to a known unit, not a wild guess; comparing estimate with measurement calibrates the body's sense of a gram, kilogram and litre and guides unit choice.

activities.title: One-step mass and volume word problems with a drawing
steps: Read a one-step problem stated in a single unit, e.g. '3 bags each weigh 250 g — what is the total mass?'
Draw a representation that matches, such as a bar model or a scaled beaker.
Write the number sentence, e.g. 3 × 250 g = 750 g, and state the answer with its unit.
Check the answer is sensible against a benchmark (750 g is less than the 1 kg bag).
activities.insight: A one-step word problem can be modelled with a drawing and solved with a single operation, keeping the unit throughout.

checkQuestion: Set out (1) a measuring jug part-filled to 340 ml on a scale labelled every 100 ml with five small unlabelled marks between (so each is 20 ml); (2) a textbook and a 1 kg bag of sugar; (3) a card reading '3 bags each weigh 250 g — what is the total mass?'. Say: 'Read how much water is in the jug and talk me through the scale; estimate the mass of the book and tell me if you'd use grams or kilograms; then solve the card.' Watch the scale-reading method and whether the estimate is sensible — not just the numbers.
checkAnswer: Works out each small mark is worth 20 ml (100 ÷ 5) and reads 340 ml; estimates the book in the hundreds of grams (≈300–800 g), choosing grams as the sensible unit and comparing against the 1 kg bag; solves 3 × 250 g = 750 g. Reasoning from the interval and from a referent, not from counting marks or guessing.
